speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ST. LAURENT (QUEBEC EAST)    REFERENCE TO ASSURANCE REPORTED GIVEN TO GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege which I believe affects every member of this house as well as the relationship between the government and the crown under our constitutional system. The question arises because of the appearance in this morning's Montreal Gazette of a letter from Mr. Leslie Roberts, the opening passage of which reads as follows:
Sir,-The Right Hon. James Gardiner's statement in the House of Commons, to the effect that the opposition has refrained from bringing down a motion of "no confidence" in the Diefenbaker government, because the Governor General exacted a promise from the outgoing prime minister that a new administration must be given an opportunity to place its program before parliament, again raises the question of impropriety on the part of the representative of the crown. It was equally improper on the part of Mr. St. Laurent, as the leader of a government, to accept such a ''deal''.
As all hon. members will realize, Mr. Speaker, this is not a correct statement of what the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) actually said in the house. The relevant statement will be found at the top of page 264 of Hansard of October 22, and reads as follows:
When the government of the day found it necessary to give assurance to the Governor General those assurances, of course, were given to the effect that we would carry on in such manner as to make it possible for the new government to have sufficient support in the house to be able to place their policies before the people of this country and carry on from there.
I should like to make it clear that no assurance whatever was asked of me by His Excellency and that no assurance was given to His Excellency by me apart, of course, from the assurance given in the public statement I made at the time I tendered the resignation of the government.
In order to avoid future misunderstanding perhaps I might be permitted to put the text of the statement on the record. It is as follows:
Although no party will have a clear majority in the new parliament the Progressive Conservative party appears to have the largest number of elected
members. In the circumstances I have reached the conclusion that the proper course for me to take was to submit the resignation of the Liberal administration to His Excellency the Governor General, which I have done today. Before doing so I advised the leader of the Progressive Conservative party of my intention, adding that of course we would carry on if he was not prepared to accept the responsibility of forming a government, but that if he does, my colleagues and I will extend full co-operation to him and his party in their arrangements for taking office so that the Queen's government can go on without interruption. I have also told Mr. Diefenbaker that I feel the Liberal members of parliament will not attempt by obstruction to prevent the new government from carrying through parliament the program it has placed before the people, though we shall, of course, exercise our right to express our views freely on the measures introduced in parliament. We feel that the growth and prosperity of the country should not be endangered by instability of government which would come from irresponsible obstruction.
What assurance I gave was, as the statement shows, given directly to the present Prime Minister and announced to the public, and I am sure that is what the right hon. member for Melville had in mind.
I referred to the same matter in my own speech on October 16 when I said, as will be found on page 46 of Hansard:
Having the reasonable assurance that the fulfilment of its promises will not be obstructed at the present session of parliament, at least by the official opposition, the government will have no excuse for any failure to carry out that program.
What I want to make abundantly clear is that there never was any question of any bargain being made between the Governor General and the outgoing administration. It is true, of course, that His Excellency was aware, as were the public, of the attitude which the members of the outgoing administration proposed to take, but there was nothing more than that.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ST. LAURENT (QUEBEC EAST)    REFERENCE TO ASSURANCE REPORTED GIVEN TO GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure we welcome the explanation of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent), but it is not sufficient.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ST. LAURENT (QUEBEC EAST)    REFERENCE TO ASSURANCE REPORTED GIVEN TO GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ST. LAURENT (QUEBEC EAST)    REFERENCE TO ASSURANCE REPORTED GIVEN TO GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I hope I never arrive at the point where I begin to separate myself from the average member in this house and adopt the attitude of being something that I am not. I just want to say that the explanation is not sufficient to meet the situation. The Leader of the Opposition mentioned one

Motions for Papers
quotation, but I would point out also that on page 264, in the first paragraph of the second column, it says:
Before there was any thought of choosing a new Liberal leader in this country the Prime Minister of the day made the announcement, when he tendered his resignation, that he had given those assurances to the Governor General.
There should not have been any mention of the Governor General in this house; that is the first principle of parliamentary government. I refrained from saying anything at the time because-well, I was shocked by the statement that was made. There could be no misunderstanding; it was made so clearly and so definitely that the explanation of the Leader of the Opposition does not meet the situation.
However, I am pleased to have his assurances in this regard which are entirely accepted, because there was no representation made to me of any such thing either by him or anyone else. I formed the government, and we asked for no such assurances. But to use the Governor General's name as an explanation for a course of action difficult to explain will also be equally inexplicable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce I wish to direct a question to his parliamentary assistant. In

Inquiries of the Ministry asking the question I do not want the house to assume that I think the minister is Santa Claus.
Is consideration being given to establishing standard grades for Christmas trees offered for sale in Canada and, if so, when is an announcement respecting specifications, etc. to be expected?

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CHRISTMAS TREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving notice of his intention to ask this question. In reply I would say that two-thirds of Canadian Christmas tree production is marketed in the United States, and a voluntary grading system is being brought into force in that market on a national basis on November 1,	1957.
Establishment of this system has been announced in the department's fortnightly publication Foreign Trade and details have been passed on to provincial governments and producers' associations.
This has renewed interest among Canadian producers in the adoption of standards covering all Canadian production. Close contact is being maintained in this matter with the provinces and the trade. The province of Nova Scotia has a voluntary grading system in existence. The trade has various grading rules in use.
The operation of the grading system in the United States will be watched with close interest. It has been introduced at a late date in the current season. If it is successful, and if general support for such a grading system develops in Canada, consideration will be given to establishing a voluntary national standard for use in this market in future years.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH U.K. PRIME MINISTER  DELEGATION TO NATO
speechtext:
Can
the Prime Minister tell the house anything about his discussions with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on Saturday and the announcement in the press that the Prime Minister himself will lead our delegation to the NATO conference in December?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH U.K. PRIME MINISTER  DELEGATION TO NATO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question of my hon. friend I wish to say this. The Prime Minister and the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, accompanied by their officials, visited Ottawa on Friday evening and part of Saturday after their conversations in Washington and we-certain of my colleagues and myself-had the opportunity to discuss the questions that had arisen in Washington.
Since the meeting of the prime ministers in London in June I have been in close touch with Mr. Macmillan and naturally I welcomed the opportunity to discuss matters of common interest.
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the foreign secretary described the conversations which they had had with President Eisenhower and Mr. Dulles. With the leave of the house I should like to table the communique issued in Washington on October 26 by the Prime Minister and the President of the United States.
Hon. members, I am sure, have been impressed by the obvious importance of this meeting and its significance in the world today. As we chatted with the Prime Minister we were greatly impressed by his appreciation of the interdependence of the free nations. That attitude is fully shared by this government. The discussions that took place in Washington were not intended to reach conclusions on matters of detail, and far less was it intended to arrive at formal and signed agreements. Just as I said a moment ago in answer to my friend the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), the destination was indicated, the direction was determined, but the means to achieve either were not in any way finalized.
I believe this conference between the Prime Minister and the President in Washington has made possible great forward steps not only by the partnership of the United Kingdom and the United States, but also in the fact that it provides an assured opportunity for many countries to broaden and strengthen their peace and security within

NATO. I think the communique makes it clear-and our conversations certainly supported that impression

not only that the government of the United States and the government of the United Kingdom were in close agreement in their approach to the basic problem of the free world but, in addition, that they determined to open a clear road on which western countries could go forward in interdependence and co-operation.
The hon. gentleman would not expect me to comment in detail, but I would draw the attention of the house to many passages in which practical measures of co-operation are indicated. Stress is once more laid on the importance of disarmament and also, in the absence of effective disarmament, on the furtherance of collective defence arrangements. Thus to the agreed ideology of the free nations there can be added a greater sharing of scientific knowledge accompanied and reinforced by co-operation in the economic field.
As Canadians we welcome this further increase of common understanding and, I believe, imaginative thinking on the part of two great powers with whom we are so closely associated. The results achieved in Washington will have particular significance in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which will be one of the principal means through which practical results can be achieved.
The hon. member mentioned the December meeting. No final determination has been made as yet regarding the attendance of heads of government, although I think we can look forward with certainty to such a meeting taking place. As he said, I propose to attend the meeting. I understand also that proposals may be sent out to the heads of NATO countries to be present at the important discussions which will inevitably take place at that time.
As far as the discussions are concerned which took place here on Friday and Saturday, they are of a confidential character and I am sure the hon. gentleman will understand that they could not properly be repeated in full detail in this house. However, I feel that a great step forward has been made, and that any of those separations that kept us apart at any time since 1945 have been closed as a result of the meetings that have taken place. The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the President of the United States met as friends who were in the war together. They met with the objective of bringing about that unity which assured peace in the days of war, and peace with victory.

Today, as a result of the meeting there, I am extremely hopeful that the essential character of what may prove to be a milestone on the pathway to security of the free world has been attained. The objective unites us. The dangers of the present give us a cohesion similar to that which existed in the days of war. With unity and firm determination I believe that the Washington meeting will in the years ahead represent a step worthy of the best in both the nations represented, and that it will in general, in its objective, be acceptable to all those nations which are joined together in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RECENT MEETING OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been asked on a couple of occasions by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) to make a statement about the meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers which was held in London from June 26 to Friday, July 5, of this year.
For me it was a novel experience, and what particularly impressed me was the atmosphere of friendship and understanding which prevailed. The meetings were presided over by Mr. Macmillan, and I was conscious of the sense of unity and common purpose which lay behind our discussions. While there was disagreement in terms on occasion there was, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) said in this house in reporting on an earlier conference, a unity in the common dedication of all members of the commonwealth to the preservation of freedom.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Meetings of prime ministers are, of course, not the only means, though they are certainly one of the means, whereby consultation is maintained among members of the commonwealth. For the first time the representative from Ghana was present and, in addition, a welcome in anticipation was given to Malaya. What took place in this regard reflected the ability of the commonwealth to adjust itself to changing conditions.
I must say a word in regard to the Prime Minister of Ghana. He not only added to the value of the discussions, but by his presence he illustrated that wise and orderly process under which the statesmen of the United Kingdom bring about the evolution to sovereign status of the various nations which previously held colonial status. This is one of the things of which I think all of us in the commonwealth can be really proud, the bringing together of peoples without regard to race or colour, and the steps taken for them to have the opportunity to become independent nations and, by their own decisions, to remain within the family of nations.
The discussions were, naturally, held in camera. A communique was issued at the end of the meetings which gives a fair impression of the scope and extent of the discussions, and, by leave of the house, I should like to table the document so it might be printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.
(For text of communique referred to above, see Appendix "B", pages 498-9.)
The subjects discussed are set out in the communique: the United Nations; the tragic events, the noble events, in Hungary; disarmament; the problems of the Middle East, the Far East and southeast Asia; and, in addition, there was a review of economic conditions and means of furthering and expanding economic development within the commonwealth.
I mentioned the United Nations. I am going to refer specifically to the clause in that connection which summarizes fairly completely the attitude of the prime ministers and the representatives of these countries within the commonwealth to that body:
The United Nations was designated to provide one of the main opportunities for the practical exercise of the principle of co-operation between nations. Experience has, however, revealed certain deficiencies and weaknesses in the functioning of the organization. The commonwealth ministers agreed that constructive action is needed to strengthen and improve the United Nations as an instrument for preserving peace, justice and cooperation throughout the world in accordance with the principles of the charter.
Because of the events in the Middle East and in Hungary in November of last year which demonstrated the strength and the
456	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry weaknesses of the United Nations, there was a feeling in several of the commonwealth countries that our ideas about its functions and procedures deserved to be reviewed. There was an underlying belief in its importance in the world, and at the same time a realization that being of human origin it had its imperfections, and that while it might be difficult to remove some of those imperfections which had been found as a result of the trial and error of experience it had nonetheless performed effectively its work in general.
I expressed the view of Canada, as I saw it, that while the United Nations had made mistakes we demanded its continuance. I also suggested that unless the tendency toward bloc voting could be checked the authority of the assembly would be undermined. In my opinion governments should vote in the light of what they see as the best interests of the world rather than as members of a voting bloc.
You will see from the reading of the communique that all were agreed about the necessity for the maintenance of the organization, and all were equally agreed that it was the duty of all governments to seek means of increasing its effectiveness.
Another question raised was that of disarmament, and an appreciation of the terrible form which a third war would take. There was no disagreement that every effort should be made to bring about a comprehensive disarmament agreement which would afford security to all nations, and that even a limited agreement would be a most desirable first step.
Since our meeting was held the subcommittee on disarmament, of which Canada is a member, ended its latest series of meetings without reporting any substantial progress, and as you know the question is now being discussed at the United Nations. My colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke in the assembly debate on Wednesday morning, and emphasized that the fundamental task before mankind is not merely to save the world from war but as well to save it from destruction.
We also discussed the question of commonwealth trade and economic relations. As my colleague the Minister of Finance mentioned in the house on Wednesday, I invited the commonwealth finance ministers to meet in Canada after the September meeting of the international monetary fund. It is my view that within the commonwealth framework a great deal more can be done than has in fact been accomplished to increase and diversify international trade and expand the 

means whereby commonwealth members can assist each other's economic development. Increased trade and co-operation in our economic relations will, I hope, be materially advanced as a result of the commonwealth trade and economic conference which is an outgrowth of the discussions which took place at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. I believe this trade and economic conference will be a practical step of value to all members of the commonwealth.
There are other though less tangible factors which bind together the members of the commonwealth. If they are not easy to measure they are nevertheless of major significance. I have in mind the general summary of the Leader of the Opposition when reporting on the last conference, when he pointed out the degree in which unity was brought about in diversity among various races and peoples in an organization that has no binding rules and no actual formation in so far as a written agreement is concerned. We are bound together, and it was extremely apparent there, in the great objectives which we hold in common. They have been said before and they bear repeating at this time and at all times: to preserve the liberty of the individual, to increase the social and economic well-being of all peoples and, above all, the need of each of the component parts working ceaselessly toward peace.
While no actual resolutions or final determinations arose out of that conference- for that is the course that is always followed in these conferences-there were in effect decisions made whereby each of the members of the commonwealth agreed without exception that only in continued co-operation and also in the maintenance of full consultation can the commonwealth achieve that destiny which is the hope of its peoples everywhere.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (for the Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 14, to provide for advance payments for prairie grain prior to delivery thereof.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am substituting today for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) who at the present time is heading our delegation at the GATT meeting at Geneva, for which he had to leave by air on Saturday. I regret and he regrets that he is not able to be here today to complete the piloting of this bill through the house.
The bill now before us appears to have the general approval of the house. On Thursday last, during the resolution stage, the Minister of Trade and Commerce outlined the main features of the bill, and hon. members who spoke had no serious criticism to offer. Some emphasized that it was a step in the right direction, but that it did not go far enough. Others considered that the 6-bushel quota was insufficient. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that no bill could be introduced in this house along this line, or along most other lines without having some people in the house ask for more.
When the vote was taken only three members of the house opposed the resolution. I hope second reading will receive the same almost unanimous consent. The House of Commons recognizes good legislation and this is good legislation; for it is designed to, and will, assist one of the most important segments of our economy. Canada's wheat industry has played a predominant part in the economic life of our country and through our export trade, has earned the income to pay for a large part of our imports.
At the resolution stage the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), suggested that the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act

Grain
should not be repealed, that it could be helpful in the early part of any marketing season. Let me make three points on this suggestion. First, the bill now before the house does not repeal the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act; second, some weeks ago, as the first step to meet the critical shortage of cash, the government proclaimed the interim financing act which provides loans to prairie producers through the chartered banks, and I am pleased to report to the house that these loans were made available by the banks at 5 per cent interest, notwithstanding the recent increase in the interest rate on other bank loans; third, while we are not proposing the repeal of this act, I do not expect it will be used extensively, if at all, when the system of cash advances comes into effect.
On many previous occasions I have expressed the view that producers should be able to obtain cash advances rather than have to seek bank loans when the elevator system is congested, and I am certain that the bank loan system will fall into disuse.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has already paid a visit to our major markets in Europe, in company with members of the Canadian wheat board. He reported to me that it was a most stimulating and on the whole heartening experience. He found that Canadian wheat is held in high regard in the United Kingdom and western European countries. Our main difficulties have arisen from the continuing encouragement that is being given to domestic production in European countries by import restrictions as well as very high support prices, and from the effects of United States barter sales. On a straight commercial basis we are fully competitive and holding our own, and we intend to remain that way. Our sales to the United Kingdom and Europe this crop year should compare favourably with last crop year.
I have referred to the surplus disposal activities of the United States as one of the main obstacles in the way of selling more Canadian wheat. It has seemed to me for some time that these activities on the part of our good neighbour to the south called for plain public speaking on our part. The Prime Minister and other members of the government have done some of that kind of speaking, and I do not think that we offended anyone. On the other hand I believe the United States administration, more of the congress and more of the American people, now know that we have a legitimate grievance.
When the joint United States-Canada committee on trade and economic affairs met in
Washington a few weeks ago the Canadian members made strong representations to the United States administration on this subject of surplus wheat disposal. In particular we protested against the effects of the barter program under which the United States exported about 90 million bushels of wheat during the past crop year. I should perhaps explain to the house that, in effect, this barter program has been only a concealed form of additional subsidy by the United States. The result has been to reduce normal United States commercial sales as well as hurt the Canadian competitive position.
We found that our United States colleagues agreed in the main with this point of view, and they affirmed to us their intention that before approving further barter transactions they would require proof that those transactions would result in additional sales. If this intention is adhered to, barter transactions are not likely to be important from now on. We also found the United States members in agreement that surplus disposal should not be permitted to interfere with normal commercial exports, and they provided evidence that their programs are being directed more and more to underdeveloped countries in acute balance of payment difficulties. We also talked with them about the tied sales provisions of surplus disposal agreements, and found that the administration had moved some way to our point of view.
I do not wish to create the impression, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government were fully satisfied with these discussions. We know that congress and not the administration makes the laws of the United States. We know too that so long as a large surplus exists in the United States and there is pressure to get rid of it there will continue to be trouble. But at least I believe we are making progress.
When the resolution preceding this bill was before the house my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a brief description of the proposal for cash advances on farm-stored grain. The bill is now in the hands of hon. members. As will be seen, this is a simple, straightforward plan. The establishment of an elaborate system of inspection of grain on the farm and the sealing of bins was considered and rejected. It would have involved an army of inspectors and a very large expenditure which in our view could not have been justified under existing circumstances. Instead, it was decided to proceed through the efficient and familiar machinery which has been in operation in western Canada for many years.
The bill proposes that the advances should be made in the same manner and through

the same channels as initial payments are now made by the Canadian wheat board, namely through the local country elevators. These elevators now buy grain for the wheat board under a handling agreement. We propose that they should make advance payments on behalf of the wheat board in a similar way.
It will be apparent to hon. members, ait was to those of us in the government, of course, that there is a considerable difference between paying for grain that has been delivered into a country elevator and making an advance on grain still on the farm and that has not yet been delivered. The government, therefore, consulted with representatives of the wheat pools, the united grain growers and the northwest line elevator association, as well as representatives of the interprovincial farm union and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I am happy to be able to report to the house that these organizations have agreed to co-operate with the government and the wheat board in making advances available through their local elevator agents and to assume a share of any losses that may result.
I have here the telegrams in answer to the request which was made to the pools, the united grain growers and the line elevator companies after discussions had been held with them and what was required of them had been outlined to them. They then went back to consult their boards of directors, and in all cases they sent favourable replies. The first one is from Ben Plumer, chairman of the Alberta wheat pool.

Then, again, I was interested in the statement he made to the effect that the legislation which I mentioned at the resolution stage- legislation which is already on the statute books-will not be repealed; in other words, the opportunity for farmers to obtain money under the farm loan legislation, as it is generally called, is still to remain. Then, too, I was pleased that at the end of his remarks he placed some figures on record in Hansard. As he stated to the house, the proper time to discuss those figures will be during the committee stage, but if we did not have them at this stage we should, of course, not have them available when we are in committee, and thus we would not be in a position to discuss them.
One part of the last submission of statistics placed before the house which interested me considerably was the set of figures which prove, apparently to the satisfaction of all members on the other side of the house, that the farms in western Canada are not as big as we sometimes hear people saying they are. We have been accustomed to hearing a great many arguments based on the idea that our farms are growing bigger and bigger, and that eventually the numbers of the farm population will be greatly decreased on that

account. But the figures contained in the table which was submitted to the house a few moments ago must remove very satisfactorily as far as I am concerned any doubts that may have been in the minds of hon. members with regard to that matter, and I am sure it will be very helpful in making decisions as to what should be done to have that evidence fairly established in our minds when we are discussing farm problems in the house.
In the latter part of his remarks the minister took occasion to address some advice to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) who is not in the house today and who probably will not be here during this discussion. I think, therefore, that I should make a few remarks with regard to what was said.

I not only listened to his speech with a great deal of interest, but I have read it over very carefully since, and I must say that the facts as he stated them and as he supported them with statistics and with quotations are very close to the facts as they exist in connection with the farmers' position in the western part of Canada, that is in the prairie section of Canada.

speechtext: His whole effort was an attempt to show that the loan system of last year was the same as cash advances. It is completely different, and the number of loans made shows it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to show that the loan system of last year was as good as cash advances as provided under Bill No. 14.
What does Bill No. 14 propose to do? It proposes to make available cash payments to a limited number of farmers in the prairie provinces; not to the whole 231,000 of them, but only to a limited number. And, further, it proposes that those cash payments should be made in limited amounts. It proposes, too, that they be made on a limited part of the farmer's production in the 1957-58 crop year and succeeding current crop years. This, in principle, is the same as the provisions in the grain producers interim finance act of 1956. That act put on limits similar to those which are put on by this act now under discussion, and I hope to be able to show that they are not likely to be greater than those under this act.

The limitations under the bank loans act of 1956 were: the loan could amount to one-half the value of the grain stored on the farm, less the return of any grain delivered in the current crop year; and the loan was limited to $3,000. In Bill No. 14 the limitations are: the amount is limited to fifty cents on wheat, 20 cents on oats and 35 cents on barley, multiplied by the quota of 6 bushels per acre, less the cash received on all but the unit quota in the current crop year. The advance is again limited to a maximum of $3,000.
Now there is one sole difference in the matter of limitation, and that was emphasized by the minister when he was speaking a few minutes ago. The first 300 bushels, that is the initial unit, is not affected by the limitation which is imposed with regard to what a farmer can obtain. But both plans limit the number of persons to be assisted, confining it to farmers having grain stored on their farms. But Bill No. 14 limits the number further to those with a current year's crop, and limits it by that quota. Then, secondly, they both limit the cash obtainable: in the case of bank loans to one-half of all grain stored on a farm with a maximum of $3,000, and in the case of Bill No. 14 to less than half the value of the grain under the 6-bushel quota in the current year with a maximum of $3,000.
I wish to say a few words concerning the statement made toward the end of the minister's address to the effect that certain payments could be made under this bill. In the first place he stated that he took No. 1 wheat as the basis upon which to do his computing of the amount. Just before I entered the chamber today I received a statement from the Department of Trade and Commerce with regard to the percentages of wheat delivered in western Canada according to grade. I am sorry I did not bring the information with me because it demonstrates that in recent years and particularly during the past year a very small percentage of the grain which has gone into elevators has been No. 1 or No. 2, that the greater proportion has been No. 3 or No. 4. It also indicates that the cash which actually does get into the hands of the farmer will be down by 11 cents, I think, if he happens to have No. 3 wheat instead of No. 1, and the amount of cash that gets into his hands will be considerably less than that if he has No. 4 wheat. As you go down the scale it becomes less and less.
When I first read the figures given-50 cents for wheat, 20 cents for oats, 35 cents for barley-I was inclined to jump to the conclusion that this was, after all, considerably below half the price if one considered the price of No. 1 wheat but I am not so

sure that my hon. friend might not be correct or nearly so when he suggests that it might be more than half the value of the grain that is obtained under those prices.

It is indicated that there will not be any competition at the local points in making loans. I am sure my hon. friend understands human nature sufficiently well to realize that he cannot maintain that position.
The elevator operators who are buying grain at points in western Canada, particularly during times when space is available, -perhaps not so much when space is not readily available-are, of course, interested in getting grain.
It should be said at this time that an elevator owner has no other way to make money. He does not speculate in grain any more; he does not buy grain at so much a bushel and sell it at so much more and make money that way. What he does is store grain and handle it, and all he gets for it are the handling charges at so much a bushel. That is the only way he can make earnings for his shareholders, or for the farmers who belong to the pool, if it happens to be the pool because, make no mistake about it, the farmers of western Canada watch the operations of the wheat pools just as closely as shareholders watch the operations of the joint stock companies. They are proud of them only when they make a return that indicates that they have not lost money. Therefore, the wheat pools are just as anxious about the charges as anyone else when they meet in those gatherings, which are composed of all the people who own and operate elevators.
When they meet in those gatherings there is an agreement between the line trade and the wheat pools as to what the charges per bushel are to be. And it is those charges per bushel that make it possible for the companies, pools or otherwise, to pay their carrying charges and have something in addition to account for to their shareholders, or to the members of their co-operative, as the case may be, and therefore, of course, there is going to be competition.
In our towns and villages there are a number of elevators. Of course, an agent in one elevator will do the best he can, and I do not think that is a bad thing for the farmers. There will be competition and that competition on the part of each will be to get the man's wheat. The best way for him to get the man's wheat is to make those advances as easily available to him as possible. When he gets started in that way he will be able to carry on right through the season and get whatever grain the man has. I am using the term "wheat" here all the way through. I should be using the term "grain" really because it applies to oats and

barley as well as to wheat. I just wanted to emphasize the fact that the grain dealer, the grain buyer, has certain responsibilities. He has a responsibility to his company to get the grain; he has a responsibility to himself and to his company not to lose money in getting it, and he is going to be a little careful about the loans that he makes.
I only recite that in order to show that there is going to be the same reason in connection with this bill for the advance to be held perhaps to a lower level, as there was in the other bill; for the banker to take care that not too much money is lost in connection with it. But what I really want to call attention to in connection with this part of the bill is that the farmers who are going to come for cash under these advances are going to be limited by something else.
This bill says that the man has his advance in the form of a cash ticket. Every farmer in western Canada knows what that means. There are very few elevators in western Canada that pay out money at any time. The elevator companies, even including the pools, are very careful about the responsibility they place on agents and they are very careful, too, about the manner in which the business is carried on. I venture to say that there is not a town or a village in western Canada where there is a bank where these cash tickets are not payable in the bank and in most places where there is not a bank there is a businessman, a merchant or some other person who has responsibilities to a bank who handles that money for the elevator company or the pool and passes it out to the farmer. One should consider that point.
Let me return to some of the criticisms that used to be made from this side of the house by those who are government members now and by our friends of the C.C.F. and of the Social Credit parties, that the banker was the last man the farmer wanted to go to. Partly because of the discussions that took place at that time but mostly because of the representations made to us by the farmers we made absolutely certain that no one had any claim on this money except the farmer. If the bank attempted to give anyone else any claim that bank did not have a guarantee at all from the government. Therefore all the money that was lent out under that plan was lent out with the absolute guarantee to the farmer that every dollar of the loan was to be handed to him. The bank could not apply it on any other indebtedness that there was to the bank with respect to the farmers' activities. That is not so in this instance.
We were told a few moments ago of one case in particular. Every farmer in western

Canada knows that under provincial law, not under federal law, there is posted in every elevator the unpaid taxes of the farmers who deliver grain to that elevator. When a load of grain is hauled in to the elevator the first thing that is taken out of the proceeds of that grain is the man's taxes, and they are paid. That was the situation when the farm loan bill was put through this house in 1956.
It was stated the other day by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) when he addressed this house that all of these things, and a great many other things, were still in the bill. They have not been in the bill since the first week it was brought into existence back in 1956. In order to have these things taken out a meeting was called in the city of Winnipeg of those who were interested. All these provisions were taken out of the administration of the act, and they could not take the taxes out of the man's small amount. I venture to say that out of the number of small farmers who were listed in the report that has been put on Hansard today a great many of them are men who owe a considerable part of what the advances will amount to in municipal taxes. Under the old legislation we maintained that since the farmer was going to get back 50 per cent of the value of the wheat that he took to the elevators, or the value of the grain he took to the elevators, over the entire period the loan was outstanding, half of that money was to be paid to the farmer, believing that the farmers in western Canada are honest, as the minister says, and believing that as they got the money they would go and pay their taxes, and not have it taken out of the amount of money that was advanced by loan then or that which will be advanced now in the form of a ticket. But when you advance it in the form of a ticket the farmer must take that ticket over to the bank and have it cashed. So far as I can find out there is nothing in this bill that makes it impossible for the banker, in these circumstances, to apply that to any account he may have in the bank against the farmer. Some of my friends object. Let them try it and see where they will get.

[DOT]-was it price support or was it mechanization, better seed and improved farming practices which brought a new day to the great wheat producing areas?
Those who have been discussing this measure have been dwelling upon the lack of cash in the hands of the farmer prior to June 10. May I say that the situation has not improved since June 10 and that this measure does not promise to help very much. The fact is that had it not been for the long-time policies of the previous government the farmers would not have survived the mechanization of their farms. I want to say that unless that legislation is kept on the statute books and functions effectively in the future the farmers will be facing that kind of bankruptcy which the leader of the government was so anxious to forecast in previous years.
What did the outgoing government do? In the first place, in 1944 they put in a system of price support to stabilize prices and it has stabilized prices. My friends say they are going to stabilize them. Might I ask this question: Are they going to stabilize them at the same level? Stabilization means keeping them the same in relation to other costs in the country. Is that what they are going to do? If they are going to try to do something different, they had better have a good look at what is being done now before they try to figure out something different. If they do so they will probably come to the same conclusion as that to which they have come on quite a number of other matters since they came into office, namely that the Liberal policies were not so bad after all.
Then what was the other matter? We did not wait until the farmers fell into the position into which they would have fallen had they mechanized their farms without any consideration being given to them in advance. In 1945 we brought in the farm improvement act. What did that act provide? It provided that a farmer could go to a bank and under a government guarantee borrow money to change over from horse-drawn equipment to tractor-drawn equipment. How much did he borrow? The farmers across this country

borrowed $653 million. From 1945 to 1956 that is the amount of money that was lent in order to help the farmers change over from one type of equipment to the other.
There have been arguments in this house from time to time as to what the farmers cash income has been; I refer not to his net income but his cash income. When we have said that it has been higher in the last five years than it had ever been in any other five-year period, people on the opposite side of the house have scoffed at the idea. But the fact is that it was higher. What proves it? This fact proves it. Of that $653 million borrowed in that time the farmers have actually paid back-that is the farmers who borrowed it-99.95 per cent of it. How could they have paid it back if they had not obtained more cash? How could they have paid it as they went along if they had not been able to take it in out of the cash income?
That is not by any means all of the money that was utilized for that changeover. The farmers who did not need to go to the bank and borrow the money paid for it as they went along under our stabilization plan. It was the support prices of the government which made this possible, along with the fact that they were working overtime, with a shortage of labour. With better methods and equipment they produced 40 per cent more than they had ever produced before in a similar period and sold their product at higher prices, particularly the wheat, than it had ever been sold since the end of the first war. Therefore they took in more cash than they ever took in before. Because they grew more than a 100 million bushels more on the average over the last five years than they had ever grown before.
They sold more in each of these years on an average than they ever sold before and so if they have now 500 or 600 million bushels of wheat in storage then it is made up of the extra 100 million bushels they have grown in each of these years over that period. Now my friends opposite are not giving them a better chance to get some money out of what they have to sell than they had before and this particularly applies to the fellow with less than enough grain to receive $3,000. More was available to the small farmer under the bank act.
I say this kind of legislation is not all the farmer needs in order to supply him with cash. In fact the regulations and legislation that we put on the statute books over the years, from the beginning of the war down to the time we went out, brought him cash, not loans; not advances but actual cash paid into his pockets totalling $1,120 millions. If our friends over there think that they

can in six months put in l/36th of that figure they will be doing about what we did. If in the year they can put in l/18th part then they will have done about the same thing and if they are fortunate enough to be in office for 22 years-which they never have been in the past-then of course they will have to at least provide the same amount to match what we have done.
The previous government was not only assisting by allowing farmers to obtain money that they would be required to pay back. We did stabilize their prices; we did support their prices; and we put them in a position to sell on this continent, on this side of the line, everything but grain at higher prices than they could on the other side of the line. In so doing we put the farmers in a position to pay out cash for the mechanization of their farms such as had never been done before.
What is the real position? Well the implement dealers have a paper and in that paper they said a few months back-and this went back to 1933-that it cost the farmer the sum of $8.40 per year in order to maintain the tools, machines and implements on his farm. Now that does not mean that the farmers out in western Canada could do that. They were taking into consideration all farmers in Canada, the man who used a hoe and a rake right up to the man who used a combine, and they said back there, when they were all using horses, that that was the position. What does it say it costs now-$555 per farmer compared with $8.40 in 1933. Of course they have been out of cash.
Looking at the conditions ahead of us the government of the day anticipated the costs of this coming change and I would like to suggest to the present government that, if they are going to remain here long enough to do any of these things, they take a good look at that legislation before they make very many changes in it, instead of going out holding up a proposal of this kind as a solution to the problems of the farmers in the west. All these measures will be required in the future and this one if it adds little will be helpful. However, Mr. Speaker, it will be helpful only in a very small way and because of small mercies I am voting for it. Nevertheless I would warn our friends opposite not to go around the country saying the other government did not do anything; the other government did not help the farmer at all and so on. The farmer will be telling them before they are through that they are on the government side now and when you are on the government side you have a responsibility and

when you have a responsibility you are likely to be the fellow who will be blamed.
I would suggest that my friends on the government side get all the facts and put them before the house and if they have legislation to bring out which would be helpful, bring it out and let us have a look at it.
