speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise in support of Bill No. 14, an act to provide for advance payments for prairies grain prior to delivery thereof. I would like to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for his introductory remarks at the second reading stage of this bill. I think he did it very concisely and gave the house the information relating to the principle of the bill. I feel it is natural that I should be pleased to speak on behalf of this bill as it has been advocated since 1943 by the C.C.F. party both in the house and throughout the country. I am pleased to support this bill also because of the fact that in the constituency of Kindersley we have the most worrisome problem we have ever had so far as congestion is concerned. I believe that in my constituency and the constituency of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), plus some of those areas around Regina, we have the largest carry through of wheat in the western provinces.
I am very pleased that at the resolution stage there was almost uniform approval of the principle of the bill. It was rather significant to notice the about-face of the Liberal party which had so vigorously fought against a system of cash advances. This remark is subject to certain exceptions because I noted as the vote was called the hon. members for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), for Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve) and Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. LaCroix) voted against it. Three members of the Liberal party have not been sufficiently informed of the problems of western Canada to appreciate the principle of the bill.
After listening to the hon. member for Melville for over an hour I am at a complete loss as to where he stands. He fortunately on two occasions mentioned he was going to vote for the bill but I suspect I will have to wait two or three days until the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) clarifies his remarks for the house.
I think the approval which the legislation is receiving should pave the way for the future legislation which the Minister of

Grain
Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) in his opening remarks last Thursday indicated was in prospect for agriculture generally.
I think in order that the house might be fully familiar with the facts confronting western farmers it would be advisable to review the conditions which exist in that area and to which the principles of this bill apply. Now anyone in western Canada knows that the problems confronting the western agriculture did not happen overnight. The problem has been building up over the past 10 years, more particularly the last five years. We know that Nero fiddled while Rome burned and in this case the Liberal administration fiddled around while western agriculture got into the difficult position it is in today.
There was a failure of that administration to maintain markets; a failure of that administration to provide leadership for international agencies, through FAO or such organizations as the food bank which we in the C.C.F. have advocated; a failure of that administration to follow the recommendations of farm organizations and to provide for legislation to prevent inflation and the cost-price squeeze.
As the result of this utter neglect over the years we have the present situation which was summed up by Dean J. R. Weir of the Manitoba university, faculty of agriculture, when he said in a recent statement that "The farmer in western Canada is caught in a squeeze between higher costs of production and reduced prices, and the small farmer is being forced to give up".
We find proof of that statement in the submission of the interprovincial farm union council to the Prime Minister of Canada when it noted that according to the census there had been a decline of more than 47,000 farm units in Canada between the census years 1951 and 1956, and that since 1946 the number of farms in Manitoba had dropped by 9.6 per cent, while in Saskatchewan the decline was 17.7 per cent.
This affords us some indication of the difficult problem which faces farmers in western Canada as a result of the cost price squeeze. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) placed on record the other day information indicating that the cost of production has increased by the phenomenal amount of 46 per cent in the last 10 years. He also pointed out that the price of wheat had declined by 21 per cent. These are the factors that have contributed to the decline in the farm population and given rise to the statement which Dean Weir of the University of Manitoba made. One cause of cost increase has been

the tremendous spiral in freight rates. In 1948 the index of freight rates stood at 100. On January 1, 1957, it stood at a colossal 219.8 and those who are from the west realize that the western farmer, the western resident, bears the brunt of this increase. Farm machinery prices have risen 94.2 per cent since 1945; the index of equipment and materials shows an increase of 72.8 per cent; and taxes and interest rates have gone up 55 per cent.
This problem is one which has been most worrisome to individual farmers because every piece of machinery they wish to buy has risen in price beyond their capacity to pay. They have been living on the depreciation of their equipment and have been unable to lay aside a fund of money adequate for the replacement of that equipment.
At the same time as costs have risen to this exorbitant level the price of wheat has fallen. I mentioned that there has been a decline in the last ten years of 21 per cent in wheat prices. Let us consider a more specific year, and compare the price figures on August 4, 1956 with those of August 3, 1957. Hon. members will find that in 1956 No. 1 Northern brought $1,733; by August 3, 1957 that had declined to $1,615, a decrease of 11.6 cents a bushel. The price of No. 2 wheat on August 4, 1956 was $1,703. On August 3, 1957 it stood at $1,575, a decline of 12.6 cents. Now let us look at the lower grades which are in such abundance in many areas; let us take No. 6. Back in August 4, 1956 the price was $1,372; on August 3, 1957 it stood at $1,185, a decrease of almost 19 cents. And these are selling prices at the lake-head, not the prices which the farmers receive for their commodity.
As a result of all this we find that there has been a reduction, between 1952 and 1956 in the net income of farmers in Canada as a whole of 18 per cent. As we enter the western areas we find that in that same period net farm income has declined in Alberta by 26 per cent and in Saskatchewan by 31 per cent. As far as can be discerned at this time net farm income in 1957 will be only one-half of the 1956 figure.
It is apparent, then, that there is great urgency that the principle of this bill should be adopted in order to afford some relief to the farmers in the western areas. We know that the predicament in which the farmers find themselves has resulted from the cost situation, plus very low delivery quotas. One matter which has been of concern to the house in recent weeks has been the phenomenal climb in unemployment figures, and I think hon. members should be aware that if farmers are forced out of business some

of them may well be added to the labour pool. The 47,000 farmers who have been forced out of business as a result of government policies are among those who potentially are contributing to the unemployment picture through no fault of their own.
We know that under present circumstances it is impossible for a young farmer to become established. The only young farmers who can become established are those who are able to take over their fathers' farms, and then only because their fathers through the kindness of their hearts have not charged for the full price of the farms or indeed, in some cases, have not charged any price at all. But to buy a farm through a mortgage company, and pay to equip it adequately with the full scale of mechanization would be quite impossible today on an economic basis. If people were satisfied to use a team of horses, as the former minister of agriculture, the right hon. member for Melville apparently is, they might be able to carry on somewhat cheaper, but we know that mechanization is necessary in order to maximize the return.
Another effect of the present economic situation is the situation of the rural community as a result of the small farm income. Those who are resident in rural communities are dependent on agriculture, and they know it full well. They have risen or fallen with the financial position of the farmers within the community. We find now that the tax picture has become very bad in many areas where delivery quotas have been extremely low; farmers are simply unable to pay taxes because, of necessity, they must reserve whatever funds they have to feed and clothe their families. This, in turn, has been reflected in the very low sales of farm equipment and machinery. In the towns within those areas we have seen many small implement agencies fold up in recent years because they were unable to survive.
The situation has been further complicated by the inequality of the quota position. I recall statements made by the former minister of trade and commerce to the effect that no effort would be made to maintain a uniform quota. At the time that statement was made, members of the C.C.F. party objected most vigorously. We said that a farmer in one area had just as much right to receive some return for his grain as had a farmer in another area. We pleaded with the government to make every effort to maintain a uniform quota. But we find that at the end of 1956 there were 103 points which ended the crop year with a 5-bushel quota, 320 which had a 6-bushel quota, and 306 which had an 8-bushel quota, while three stations were closed.
Grain
In 1957 there was an effort to maintain a uniform quota and 431 delivery points ended up with a five-bushel quota and 666 with a six-bushel quota with five stations being closed. I hope it is understood by all hon. members that merely because a marketing point is given a quota this does not mean that all farmers in that area have marketed the full amount of their quota. It is conceivable that a quota would be given to a marketing point in the last two weeks of the crop year and farmers in outlying areas or those who did not have adequate transportation would not have the opportunity of delivering their grain before the space became congested.
These inequalities in the quotas have resulted to a large degree from the failure of the Liberal government to maintain a transport controller, someone who is charged with the responsibility of seeing that railway box cars were in position to meet the demand and that they were not sent to points that did not require them. It has also been as a result of the system of allowing milling companies to skim off all the high protein wheat. I have found that the practice in the past has been to allow mills to take their wheat from whichever elevator had wheat of the highest protein content. The net result of this, of course, has been to leave the wheat of low protein content to the export trade. This is a matter which deserves investigation.
Bill No. 14 will certainly help to resolve this problem of unequal quotas because if a farmer is in a position to receive some money for the grain he has grown but is unable to sell, it is not as vitally important that the delivery quotas be maintained at the same level. In the same breath, however, I would point out that every effort must be made to maintain a uniform quota. At the same time it is apparent that if through some slip or other the quotas are not maintained at exactly the same level the same degree of hardship will not accrue to the farmers.
The proposal indicated in Bill No. 14, as the Minister of Agriculture pointed out, will supply money to the farmer now rather than his having to wait until the quota becomes available. In the opinion of the western Canada farm organizations and in the opinion of farmers I have talked to this represents a tremendous improvement over the bank loans legislation which was devised by the previous administration. Hon. members who were here at that time will doubtless recall the battle which the farm organizations put up and which we in this group voiced in the house in opposition to the farmer paying interest on what were in fact his own wages. I believe it

Grain
is immaterial whether the bank loan legislation is left on the statute books, which matter seemed to be the major plank in the address of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), because if it is left operative no one will use it in any case since they will now have the opportunity as a right to receive a cash advance on their grain.
Bill No. 14 will provide temporary relief for those who are unable to deliver their grain which will give them an opportunity to restore their credit. In all fairness to the legislation I think we cannot build up our hopes too high in terms of thinking of it as cure-all legislation. After all, it is a temporary palliative and it is like a person taking an aspirin tablet when he has influenza; it will make him feel a little better for the moment but will not cure the malady from which he is suffering. The system of cash advances will certainly not correct the cost-price squeeze in which the farmer finds himself but it is welcome as a temporary relief for those who cannot realize any money whatever from their grain.
I was pleased that the Minister of Agriculture made reference to the erroneous news reports which had been distributed through eastern Canada indicating that the cost of this proposal would be the outlandish figure of $100 million to $150 million. In fact on the C.B.C. television news on Thursday I personally heard the newscaster report that the total cost of the program would be between $100 million and $150 million. I think it is most unfortunate that this erroneous information was disseminated in that manner. As I calculate it the cost of interest charges will be approximately $2| million and perhaps much less than that. There is a popular misconception which is all too generally held of conditions in western Canada and a similar misconception exists concerning what this government and previous governments have done to assist the farmer in western Canada.
I wonder what will be the position under this proposal of the farmer who has no grain, and indeed there are many in this position. At the end of the crop year there was an indication that 48 per cent of the farmers in western Canada would have no carryover at the end of July and of the 42 per cent that had a carryover 25 per cent had less than 300 bushels. It is apparent that it does not matter what type of cash advance proposal the government is able to introduce it will be of no assistance to the large number of farmers who have no grain and who are confronted with a serious problem.
There are some aspects of the bill on which I would like some information but I know

this must wait until we reach the clause by clause discussion of it. However, I might just mention one or two points. I am interested in learning what will be the position at the end of the crop year of the farmer who has taken an advance and is unable to deliver grain to retire the advance. Another aspect that aroused my curiosity as I read the bill was the priority given in it to the bank loans legislation. If I understand it correctly it is apparent that it cannot do any particular good to the farmer. Another factor I will want to discuss is the responsibility of the elevator agent in making loans and what his responsibility will be in seeing that the loans are repaid. I am simply mentioning these questions now so the minister will be aware of a possible complaint in these general terms.
I do not wish to take up any more time of the house because I think it is important that this bill be enacted as soon as possible so the benefits under it can be extended to the people of western Canada. I think the bill is good and one that should become permanent legislation. In saying this, however, I should point out that the system of cash advances will not resolve the basic problem of the cost-price squeeze. It does not matter how many cash advance proposals are devised by the government, they will not solve the dilemma of the farmer whose net returns for his products are not great enough to equal the cost of production. This must be resolved through the adoption of an agricultural program that will give to agriculture its fair share of the national income.
It has been advocated that a deficiency payment of 20 cents a bushel could be made to all farmers and that would come close to solving the problem at the moment as far as the western farmer is concerned but we must eventually solve it by finding additional markets for our wheat.
I think the proposal has been well summed up in a statement made by Mr. J. H. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and because it is stated so succinctly I wish to place it on the record. Mr. Wesson said:
The proposal to make cash advances on farm-stored grain will provide some cash income immediately. If the legislation provides for advances through elevator agents, as suggested in newspaper reports, this money will be widely and readily available to farmers. However as the wheat pool has repeatedly emphasized in discussions with the government and members of parliament cash advances do not solve the basic problem of western grain growers.
I think all hon. members should give serious consideration immediately to passing this proposal and that we should then review

Grain
agricultural conditions in all of Canada. I am not unmindful of the fact that the farmers in other areas are suffering hardships from this same price-cost squeeze. Perhaps the unique set of circumstances, the benevolent years we have had, have caused the tremendous buildup of grain in western Canada; but we do know when we have a situation which requires a fruit grower of British Columbia to spend three boxes of apples to buy one bushel of wheat and a wheat farmer in Saskatchewan to spend three bushels of wheat to buy one box of apples, something is drastically wrong and that governmental action must be taken at an early date to resolve this basic problem for the benefit of all Canada.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in this debate on second reading of Bill No. 14, to provide for advance payments for prairie grain prior to delivery thereof.
Before starting my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) on the very able way in which he presented this bill this afternoon. I could not help but feel that there had been quite a change in the way bills were presented to members of parliament sitting in opposition groups.
The arguments for cash advances on farm-stored grain have been presented to this house for many years and they have been presented already in the course of this debate and at the resolution stage. Two years ago, and again last year, extensive debate was carried on on a bill called the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act. When that bill was up for discussion we in this group opposed it on the ground that we did not feel that that particular bill, or the farm loan wheat bill, as we called it, would give the farmers of western Canada the cash they would need to carry on their operations.
I was very much interested in the remarks of the former minister of agriculture this afternoon. In his remarks the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) reminded me very much of his behaviour in previous sessions when he was minister of agriculture and presented the problems of agriculture to the house. It was definitely one of confusion with no information being given. In previous sessions we urged he former minister of trade and commerce to institute a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain which would assure the grain farmers of western Canada a temporary measure of relief from the critical financial position they found themselves in. We still feel that this measure, which is up for second reading today and which is being discussed this afternoon, is nothing
more than a temporary measure and it will be only of some immediate assistance to the grain farmers of western Canada.
Regardless of how long we argued with the former minister of trade and commerce he did not see fit to institute a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain. This afternoon the former minister of agriculture did point out that they might have done it this year had they been on the government benches. That situation was very capably handled by the western farmers on June 10 of this year, because the province of Alberta returned only one Liberal member to this house. Therefore, the farmers of Alberta were very definite in their opinion of the agricultural policy, if you can call it a policy, of the former administration.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to see that so many members of the official opposition at the present time see fit to support this legislation in a placid type of way. This change of heart forecasts a much better deal for all those engaged in agriculture, because it is now apparent that the vast majority of the members of this house are prepared to support progressive legislation which will place the farmers of Canada in a better financial position.
My colleague, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), last week placed on record the position of the Social Credit group in the house, with respect to this piece of legislation; and since we feel that there is a degree of urgency associated with the passage of this bill it is not my intention to take up too much of the time of the house this afternoon. However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that we view this legislation as being only a temporary solution, one which will bring a measure of immediate relief to the grain farmers of western Canada and not one which will provide a permanent solution.
Our farm population is steadily decreasing and the average age of those engaged in farming in western Canada is steadily rising. If this situation is permitted to continue we shall quite possibly find ourselves concerned, not with so-called man-made surpluses but with actual shortages of foodstuffs. Young people for very obvious reasons, are not staying on the farms, largely because of the fact that they are all too well acquainted with the uncertainty attached to that type of life. They are not prepared to work from dawn to dark, to gamble with weather and so forth for the meagre returns which their fathers have received in the last few years. Instead of following in their fathers' footsteps they have entered other occupations in which they are assured of a larger measure of security and greater financial returns.

Grain
For years farmers have been faced with ever increasing production costs and a continual decline in the selling price of the goods which they had to sell. Again, Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in the remarks of the former minister of agriculture this afternoon. He pointed out that the previous administration had spent millions of dollars to aid agriculture. It is true that the previous administration passed the Agricultural Prices Support Act in 1944. However, Mr. Speaker, in the first ten years of its operation it cost the people of Canada 15c. per person per year to support the price of agricultural goods right across Canada, a huge amount of money in the eyes of the former minister of agriculture, but certainly a meagre sum to those who received the benefits of that act.
Farm organizations right across Canada have constantly brought this situation to the attention, not only of the previous administration but of the public at large, with little or no apparent effect until recently. I would say that the passage of this legislation should be looked upon as a major victory for the farm organizations and those so active in presenting their views during the last few years. It is to be hoped that the forecast long-range plan to stabilize the agricultural industry will soon be brought before us for consideration. The need for this particular legislation has been recognized by all parties and by practically every member in this house.
The interprovincial farm union council, in its brief which was presented to the government on August 15 of this year, advanced many strong arguments as to why something must be done to improve the position of those engaged in agriculture. They point out that in the last 18 months agricultural production costs have risen 16.7 per cent, that the retail price of bread has increased 2 cents per pound, that the price of wheat has decreased by 23 cents per bushel; that the interest rates on loans to the Canadian wheat board have increased; that the increase in the value of the Canadian dollar has had an adverse effect upon the farmers of Canada.
We of this group are not prepared to admit that there is an actual surplus of our agricultural products at the present time, including even wheat. I believe the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations pointed out last year that we had in the world at that time only a three months supply of wheat for our wheat consuming population. This amount should not be classed as a surplus. I am sure there is not one farmer in Canada today who would like to think in terms of having only a three months supply of food on hand for his

stock. The fault lies partially in the fact that the marketing policies which the previous administration followed were definitely faulty, and instead of being able to get our grain to the hungry people throughout the world the farmers of western Canada were called upon to finance practically the whole burden of this unneeded surplus.
This legislation will provide a measure of relief but we do hope that the new government will adopt trading policies which will enable our producers to sell their goods at a reasonable price. We recognize that all cannot be changed overnight but we suggest to the government that it is not fair to expect the farmers of western Canada to finance any great portion of this surplus. It is for this reason that we of this group have constantly emphasized the need for the establishment of government-owned terminal elevators throughout the west.
The box car situation in the west remains one of confusion. The quota position throughout my area is worse today than it was a year ago. It is all very well for government spokesmen to point out that export sales are up, but to the average farmer that means very little. He still sees his granaries full of wheat. He is still forced to build new ones to accommodate this year's crop. He is still forced to accept his income in a bit now and a bit later process. I submit that there is no wage earning group in Canada today which would be pleased or happy to receive its salary on the instalment plan, and that is exactly what the farmer of western Canada has been forced to do for years. The farmers are constantly plagued with unpaid bills and are always short of cash. These are realities, and unless we want a complete collapse in our grain-growing industry immediate and definite steps must be taken.
I was very sorry to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) state in reply to a question of mine the other day that the government had not seen fit to re-establish the position of transport controller. We have argued in the house for some years now that there was need of a transport controller, a person charged with the responsibility of seeing that there was an equitable distribution of box cars in the west at all times; and not only charged with the responsibility of seeing that this happened but given the authority to carry out his responsibility. I feel we can look forward to another crop year of confusion as far as the box car situation is concerned.
Many people across Canada are of the opinion that the farmer is getting something

Grain

AFTER RECESS

he is not entitled to, that the farmers of Canada are always demanding and giving very little. In the May 10 issue of the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget the editor of that paper put before the public a little article entitled "Fair Play". He pointed out in this issue that utterances and writings across Canada continue to condemn the farmer for his approach to his present economic difficulties. He pointed out that it is said that farmers must stop demanding help, that the price of wheat must come down, that the law of supply and demand must be recognized, that an industry cannot be bolstered by subsidies, that agriculture no longer is indicative of the prosperity of Canada and that other industries should not be penalized by subsidies to agriculture.
These and many other comments are frequently heard from coast to coast in Canada. It is obvious from such comments that many people still do not understand or appreciate the position of the western farmer. Traditionally the western farmer has spurned aid and has preferred to stand on his own feet. Free trade has been the slogan of the farmer of the west since the early days. That, however, is not the way the people of Canada want things. They have decided to protect pratically every other industry in Canada from foreign competition. If the law of supply and demand is going to be set aside for others, then the farmers too must play under the same rules.
His costs have skyrocketed because of the high prices others have been permitted to charge in a protected market. He cannot be adequately protected by tariffs because what the farmer produces, particularly wheat, are export commodities. It is neither illogical nor unfair that a small portion of the tax dollar collected from the profits of those who have benefited at his expense be used to support agricultural prices. Agriculture may no longer determine the degree of the nation's prosperity but it is still vital in maintaining it. Ours is not a free and competitive economy but rather a regulated one. The rules that assure the prosperity of some should guarantee at least the survival of others. The moment that all Canadians agree to absolutely free and unrestricted trade so that the farmer can buy his requirements from the cheapest source, price supports'for agriculture will not be needed. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that that pretty well points up the position facing those engaged in agriculture not only in western Canada but from coast to coast.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to make my first remarks in this house as the new member for Qu'Appelle I cannot help but say in all seriousness that this legislation which has been introduced into this house and which carries my name along with that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) represents to many of us a great moment in this country's history.
I think I can say honestly that for seven years this has been one of the subjects on which I have spoken and expressed myself all through the western part of Canada. Hence it is not inappropriate that as the new member for Qu'Appelle I should be making my first remarks in this house on the subject of wheat. A predecessor of mine who came from there was a man by the name of Ernest Perley. He represented Qu'Appelle during the years 1930 to 1945. His very name stood for wheat. Every time he rose in his place in this House of Commons, both on this side of the house and on the other side, the members of the house knew what the subject was going to be when he rose to speak. I hope that tonight, Mr. Speaker, my remarks here will do justice to his memory.
The significance of the cash advance to the western farmers can be understood only through knowledge of some of the background of what has happened over the last 20 years. I do not intend to speak at any great length. I just wish to emphasize and to point out the highlights of this background so that hon. members from all parts of Canada may understand the deep feeling with which those of us from the west approach this matter.
The depression was not only a depression to us in western Canada; it was a double depression. All parts of the world had a decline of prices and unemployment, but in addition, we had drought and no crops and the situation hit us doubly hard. In addition, the depression was followed by war in which the people in western Canada were asked to make sacrifices along with the rest of Canada, something which has peculiar connotations today. This part of Canada was put under price control as well as the rest of Canada. Our wheat price was set for that wheat which was sold abroad and a special price of 77i cents a bushel was set for that grain which was sold for consumption in Canada. During the war we were asked to join in that war effort. Not only were we asked to send our young men and our young women into uniforms and into factories in central Canada,

Grain
enough security there to protect any average creditor, because those of us who come from the west know the significance of the permit book. The only way you can beat this legislation-I am speaking now to those who come from areas outside western Canada-is to quit farming because then you will not have a permit book. We who are living under the western Canadian system know what that means.
Now this concludes that part of my remarks on this subject. I repeat that it is not the fault of the western farmer that his markets have been lost; it is not his fault that the grain storage is blocked in the elevator. He has cut his acreage down and has made every effort he can to get out of this mess. We have to meet the situation left on our doorstep by the previous administration.
There has been some discussion-I am simply amazed at this-as to whether the farm organizations and the farmers generally want cash advances. Let me assure my friends in this house, in all parties and from all parts of the country, that the great majority of the western farmers-I would say 95 per cent-want a system of cash advances. There is no argument about that in western Canada and this whole issue tht has been kicked around in the house today, makes me wonder. I did some reading between the closing of the house at six o'clock and the opening at eight o'clock and I picked up a copy of the Leader-Post dated November 12, 1955, where I found this heading "Farmers Mass Meeting ask for Cash Advances". There was another statement where the former minister of agriculture was speaking-but I will leave that for a moment and will come back to it later because I see the former minister is now in his place.
I have had some experience with this matter. I have seen resolutions go through by every political party in western Canada, including the Liberal party, in support of cash advances; I have seen these resolutions go through every board of trade in support of cash advances; I have seen the legislatures of western Canada pass resolutions in favour of cash advances. I do not know of a farm organization today in Saskatchewan which lets its body politic or rank and file get together and discuss these matters which is not in support of cash advances. That is the feeling on this matter in the west. I have heard in this debate some remarks to the effect that one party has been supporting this legislation since 1952 and I have just finished saying that I have heard resolutions put through by every party. I thought it might be appropriate at this time, in view of the fact that the leader of the Conservative [Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).l
party of a few years ago is not now in this house, to read the remarks of the Hon. George Drew who was then leader of the official opposition contained in his first speech in the new session of parliament in the fall of 1952. It is reported in Hansard of November 24, 1952.
Farmers are finding it impossible in many cases to deliver their grain to the market, we are informed, no matter what steps are being taken. The whole system of handling and distribution has broken down. The government, no matter what its explanation may be, has failed to take effective steps to provide for the handling of grain, in spite of the knowledge many months ago, and the warnings many months ago, that this situation was going to arise. In western Canada today there are many farmers, with huge quantities of wheat and other grains worth considerable sums of money, who are unable to get money at this time to cover their harvesting and living expenses because of their inability to deliver that grain to market.
This is a situation with which the government should deal immediately. It is urgent and calls for attention without delay.
Now this was November 24, 1952. If that situation was urgent in 1952 it is doubly urgent today and I am making no apologies for reading into the record the words of the then leader of the opposition.
If for no other reason than the passage through this house of this bill on cash advances, this government deserves the support of the people of Canada. There is a real need here, and we have met this real need and we have shown our determination to put into action what we have preached.
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated, I believe, that I wish to be fair in these matters. I have said that all parties in western Canada supported this proposal to make cash advances. It was only in the last election that people realized that by dividing their votes among the parties they would defeat this end, and they began to rally behind the party which is now led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Mr. Speaker, in this debate we have heard members of the official opposition declare their support for cash advances. That was after June 10. This conversion is remarkable, and I cannot but recall the days of the bank loan. I am going to pick up a copy of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix dated November 9, 1955, and, again, I will read just the headlines:
Gardiner Defends "Howe Plan" Giving Bank Loans to Farmers.
At that time I was suspicious that Mr. Howe was getting his throat cut from ear to ear, because according to the headline this was not the policy of the government. Back in 1955 this was described to western farmers as "The Howe Plan" and indeed Mr. Howe did get his throat cut from ear to ear on

June 10. Now we have heard in this house today a declaration that this is now good legislation, and the former minister of agriculture is defending what two years ago was the Howe plan.

That is for No. 1 northern, and I hope I may be allowed to table these figures. The next set of figures relates to No. 4, and I find on looking at my table that a man on 50 acres receives 73 per cent of his initial price; the percentage is higher. this had been the request of the farm organizations over the last several years. I believe that is a fair statement.

In any case,

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get to the burden of my remarks, which are going to be very brief this evening, I should like at the outset to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), who this afternoon for the very first time since I have been in this house at

least placed on the record in unmistakable terms the position of the western farmer, in so far as the arguments put forward are concerned that he is a man who is engaged in an industry and has been asking the people of Canada to support him over the years. I think the minister and the government should be commended because never before has the government gone out of its way to place the true picture of western agriculture before this house and to give the members of eastern Canada some indication of just what is involved in farming in western Canada.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal for a moment with some of the arguments put forward this afternoon in defence of the former bank loan administration. The former minister of agriculture, the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), tried to point out that this legislation was not better than the former bank loan legislation. Well, in so far as the merits of it are concerned and the money that is going to be put in the hands of the western farmer is concerned, I would wholeheartedly agree, but there is a considerable difference. First of all, the banks are not involved and that is very important. The elevator agents are going to be responsible for carrying out the mechanics of this proposition and, of course, the fact that there is no interest charge is of tremendous importance.
While I am not happy about the legislation as a method of doing something concrete for western agriculture, I am going to say that it is a lot better than what we have had before and it is a great deal better than any of the plans that are being put forward by certain other people in this country as a method of helping out the farmer in th dilemma in which he finds himself today. For the benefit of the Liberal party in this country I should like to put on record one of the plans which is being put forward by a certain individual who was very close to the Liberal party prior to the last election. Here it is. It is an offer to buy wheat provided that the farmer delivers it to a point specified in this advertisement for a cent a pound. This applies to No. 5 and No. 6 wheat which today are selling on the market for 97 cents a bushel. This certain individual is offering 60 cents a bushel, a cent a pound. Things are so bad that the farmers are taking advantage of these propositions which are being put forward by certain unscrupulous people in this country.
It is even worse when you follow it through to its logical conclusion. Here is an individual who in effect is saying to the farmers: if you will buy a refrigerator from

me I will take half cash and the remainder in wheat at a cent a pound. First of all, he hikes up the price of his refrigerator by $80 and the upshot of the whole proposition is this, the refrigerator that he is selling for $448 brings him a net profit of $225 at the farmers' expense. Who is putting forward this plan? Nobody else, Mr. Speaker, but the former representative in this house from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, Mr. Ross Thatcher, protege of the hon. member for Melville who went around the province of Saskatchewan saying, "You should elect this man because he is an important man in the Liberal party and he will do great things for western agriculture."
I was very concerned and not a little amused this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. member for Melville was concerned and shed a lot of tears about the impossible position the elevator agents were going to be put in because of this measure. He said, "You are placing them in a position where they are going to have to indulge in certain questionable practices; they are going to go out and they are going to have to bid for this grain in ways that possibly would not be too acceptable."

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I did not call any of the practices that I discussed questionable practices.

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext:
I well remember last year, Mr. Speaker, and the year before, that the opposition today, when they were on the government side of the house, used every devious means-and I do not think it is too strong a word-to keep producers from delivering grain to the elevator of their choice. Whenever a piece of legislation was introduced in this house suggesting that the farmers should be able to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice the government of the day voted solidly against it. Now, apparently, they are worried about the elevator agents. I do not think the elevator agents or the people of Canada are going to appreciate the reflection which was cast on the elevator agents by the remarks of the former minister this afternoon.
I have said that I am going to have to agree with one thing the hon. member said. I agree wholeheartedly with him that the government is being dishonest when they say that the measure before this house is a cash advance measure. It is nothing of the kind; it is a loan. Before they are finished with this piece of legislation I should like the government to explain to me and to the party which I represent why they did not introduce an honest cash-advance piece of legislation. What is a cash advance? Well, any farmer in this house knows that any time he takes hogs or cattle to the market to
Grain
sell he is invariably asked whether he would like an advance. It is a common practice. In many instances I have done it myself. I have said, "Yes, I will take $100." But when I get my returns they show the full amount less the advance that I received.
Why could the government not have done the same thing in this legislation? Why could they not say to the farmer, "We will give you 50 cents for the wheat you have and when you haul it in here we will give you the remainder?" That would be the end of the transaction. It seems rather foolish to me to say to the farmer, "You owe us money." The farmer does not owe the wheat board any money on a bushel of wheat when he has received only 50 cents. The wheat board owes him money. Does it not seem foolish that when he delivers his wheat, in spite of the fact that the wheat board owes him the difference between what he received, 50 cents, and the initial price, which may be $1.20, to say to the farmer, "Oh, yes, we owe you 61 cents or 62 cents, but until you pay us the 50 cents we will not pay you any more?" In other words, they are saying, "You pay us back the 50 cents and we will pay you the $1.20." This seems very strange to me.
What would happen under the wheat board system of marketing today if when you hauled your grain to the elevator you received the initial payment of $1.20 and some time during the winter you were to get an interim payment of, say, 10 cents a bushel?
Would it be reasonable to say to the farmer, "We will not pay you the 10 cent interim payment until you pay us the $1.20 that we paid you initially and then we will give you $1.30"? I should like the government to explain the kind of reasoning they used in arriving at this formula.
So, Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to say, as I said in the first instance, that the bill is going to put a little cash in the hands of farmers who are badly in need of it, but I think the important part of it is that it is going to equalize quotas. As long as we have a quota system we are going to be faced with the problem of inequality under that system. As I see it, it cannot be avoided. The measure we are dealing with will do something to equalize the quota system. While we are not satisfied with the legislation, we are going to approve of it because we see in it something a great deal better than anything that has been proposed in the house prior to now.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) referred in his closing remarks to the imbalance of purchasing power in certain segments of our

Grain
population. For that reason I should like to make some observations inasmuch as I come from a province other than those that are covered by the bill. I supported the resolution when it was introduced and made the request that the bill be altered so that primary producers in all the provinces rather than in a limited area might be included under its provisions.
Some members may feel that it would be impossible to have the legislation operate in the province of Ontario but in that province we have marketing agencies which could act as the liaison between the government and the primary producers. I am sure such agencies could meet the requirements of this legislation. Some representatives of these organizations came to Ottawa shortly after the election and met different members of the government for the purpose of placing the position of the primary producers before them. For example, representatives of the Ontario wheat producers association, accompanied by members of the federation of agriculture from several counties in southwestern Ontario and by supporters of the government from the area that they represented, requested the government to take action regarding the wheat problem in Ontario. The soybean marketing board and the horticultural council representing the fruit and vegetable growers sought assistance of a similar nature.
I am sure hon. members will agree that if the industry was in a healthy position these busy men would not have approached the government as many of the problems racing the industry have been resolved by action taken by their own associations. Recently the farm loan board made the statement that farm loans have increased 60 per cent compared with a similar period a year ago. I think that points out very definitely that agriculture as a whole certainly is not in as healthy a position as it might be.
On October 24 I asked the minister who is piloting the bill in the house tonight if he would before the conclusion of the speech from the throne debate consider the possibility of bringing in legislation to stabilize farm prices, and I was referring at that time to the commodities I mentioned a while ago. My reason for asking the question was simply that many of the commodities now being harvested are not bringing prices that are consistent with good farming practice. I also mentioned the very low price of corn. I learned about this particular instance from a person who knew the farmer who sold the corn, and the net to the producer was 46 cents a bushel.
I contend that if the provisions of the bill regarding cash advances were extended to [Mr. Huffman.!
the producers of corn in the area in which it is produced the producer might receive by way of a cash advance almost as much as he received for his whole crop and at the same time had to lose complete control of it. The corn could be placed in storage where it could dry naturally. It would improve in quality and we would be able to feed a supply of corn into the different channels that require it, mainly the starch companies and the breakfast food companies. Unfortunately there are men who need ready cash in Ontario and the six other provinces not covered by the bill which will only give assistance to the three western provinces.
The reason I asked a question on October 24 was that it did not seem to me that the provisions of this bill would cover the situation and I wanted to know whether the government would bring down soon a stabilization program that would meet conditions such as I have outlined.
This afternoon many hon. members spoke about the small farmer. I am sure everyone realizes that in the other seven provinces of the dominion there are many small farmers. I know that is so in our province. Consequently, I should like to appeal to the government again to assist small farmers in every part of Canada. This afternoon the bill was termed a lifesaver.

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext: With a hole in it.

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext:
Someone says that there is a hole in it. This bill is really a lifesaver with a hole in it and seven provinces of the dominion are going to get only the hole.
I have talked to farmers from western Canada who are in Ottawa at this time. I have discussed with them our problem and their problem. They agree that we have a justifiable claim for the same consideration as is provided for western producers by this bill.
I have every sympathy for those who need the provisions of this legislation. I am sure the producers of western Canada will honour their obligations. I was very glad to hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources say that because we also feel that in this industry there is honour and that our farmers will certainly meet their obligations, both those that will be incurred under this measure and those now in force under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act.
It has been estimated that between $100 million and $150 million will be advanced to growers without interest. Again I say that if the government would extend similar provisions to the seven other provinces there would be a good deal more purchasing power immediately available to the many who are

in need of ready cash. Part at least of this year's production would be covered.
Having supported the resolution so that I might have a look at the bill in its final form, I must now register disappointment on behalf of those I represent and those who I feel are neglected. The bill has been called discriminatory by some but I must confess that it has all the earmarks of segregation by legislation.

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this bill I derive a certain amount of pleasure because I think it is one of the most important bills that has been introduced in my short term here in so far as western farmers are concerned. I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is to be complimented on the able way in which he presented this bill. It is refreshing indeed to find a minister who is not afraid to take the wraps off his bills and to present them in their true light. To the farmers who were obliged to indulge in that questionable luxury of borrowing their own wages at five per cent interest I am sure it will be refreshing to see that at long last they have access, in a limited way at least, to the fruits of their labour.
I think this bill goes a long way toward alleviating the stress on the farmer and his economic problems. Nevertheless, it is only a palliative and a means to an end. I hope this government will not fall into the state of complacency that seemed to be the mark of the previous government and feel that by bringing this worthwhile measure before the house, they have done all that is required of them. Basically I think this points up one important point, namely that the cure or solution of our problems does not lie in administering palliatives such as this but rather in coming to grips with the problem of marketing the produce of the biggest partner in Canadian business, namely agriculture.
While this measure, in a sense, helps the farmers, it does not

fortunately or unfortunately-help all of them. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are many small farmers who-whether because of taking the advice of members of the previous government and adhering to the technique of diversification or whether it was brought about by necessity-were forced to go out of wheat growing to a large degree. I note that this measure will not help them. For the sake of self-preservation they were obliged to indulge in diversification. Many of them diverted their activities into livestock and dairying and many of them resorted to the growing of seeds and other grain. In my constituency I find that many
Grain
farmers, because of their desire to make an honest living, started growing rape seed as a means to an end. They found that by growing rape seed they would get some semblance of a just return for their efforts.
However, it was only a short time until they found that there was a roadblock in their way. I refer to the discriminatory freight rates that prevailed. It may be argued that this matter is not relevant to the bill before the house. However, I think it is relevant because that was a direct substitute for a livelihood in many instances in my constituency. I think' no hon. gentleman here can suggest that it is desirable or necessary for a freight rate to be raised three times when it related to a new outlet whereby a farmer could have the right to live. I cannot see any moral or economic justice in demanding a freight rate of 70 cents per hundred, when it is obviously fair to charge only 22J cents on flax or other grains. I fail to see why it is necessary to charge 70 cents in one instance and, as far as the rate to the British Columbia coast is concerned, 64 cents. I think it is the responsibility of this government to see to it that more justice prevails at that level. Are we going to deny to the small farmer the right to diversify and to grow crops that will not clash with the best interests of everyone concerned and, through that medium, to minimize his necessity to avail himself of cash advances?
I know the benefits accruing from cash advances. I know that when the farmer gets money the merchants, of which I was one for a number of years, certainly receive the benefit of it. The minute the farmer gets a dollar business picks up almost overnight. When his conditions are depressed, by the same token the merchant's business is depressed. I think it would be a happy situation and a desirable one if, in spite of this wonderful bill, the government would give some more consideration to these small farmers who are not privileged to cash in on these cash advances. I think it is their responsibility. I think they should place more emphasis on finding markets and on seeing to it that something is done by the board of transport commissioners or the railroads or whoever is responsible. In the final analysis it is the responsibility of this parliament. I think they should see to it that consideration is given to the little farmer who because of adhering to the advice and wishes of the government has tried to eke out an existence through some other means.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be brief in the few remarks I wish to make on this piece of legislation. I also should like to compliment

Grain
the government on bringing in this measure of loans to farmers or, as they would rather have it put, cash advances. It is more needed this year than at any time previously for the simple reason that our grain is moving at a slower rate than it has ever moved before. A good three-quarters of the delivery points for grain in the west are not even in the position where they can accept the first one-bushel quota. This fact puts the farmers in those areas in a position where they are in receipt, in the first three months of the crop year, of something of the order of $300 or $350, depending on what kind of grain they have to deliver. This amount is not much more than will provide lubrication for the machinery for removing the crops from the field and further cash is definitely needed from some source or other to take care of the balance. This is a palliative which will help, in its way, those farmers who have grain. Of course for those farmers who have no grain-and they comprise a considerable number in the west this year because of drought and periods of continuous rain which have spoiled what in many cases was a fairly good crop-other remedies are necessary.
My friend from Saskatchewan, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) in his opening remarks said that this is a great moment in Canadian history. I am in entire agreement with that statement because I think this is the first time the Conservative party has made a gesture towards finding a solution of the problems of the farmers in the west. There was something previously which one might call a gesture when the last Conservative regime under Mr. Bennett gave five cents a bushel to those farmers who had wheat. At that time about one farmer in a hundred had any wheat so the other 99 went without.
These pieces of legislation are both based upon the cornerstone of Tory philosophy-to those who have shall more be added unto. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources said quite candidly this was not supposed to fix up all the western farmers' problems but I note that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has in view more permanent relief for them and has a really basic solution for their problems when he tells them they should not raise wheat at all. That is certainly a way to get away from their trouble. It may also be a way to remove the troubles from the shoulders of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I note that he did not say in his remarks made to a meeting of the dairy council in September that he had any suggestion as to what they should do to make a living when they quit growing wheat.

Well, if you are going to carry that kind of remedy to its logical conclusion you will tell the farmers of Prince Edward Island they should not grow potatoes and the fishermen of the maritimes they should not catch fish. We have to find a longer-ranged remedy than that implied by these suggestions because the prairies are suited to growing wheat and it would not be very practical to try growing coconuts there and raising wheat in the South Sea islands. We grow these things where they will grow. However, this piece of legislation will help in some areas where farmers have wheat and to that extent I am happy to support it.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks in connection with this bill under discussion will not be long. Previously I have given my view that this cash advance legislation is needed quickly as a stop-gap to assist the farmers of western Canada. The marketing of Canadian wheat is the problem which faces the government and we have heard on more than one occasion remarks from the government benches that the government is doing everything it can to sell Canadian wheat and to regain lost markets.
On October 18 in this house I questioned the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) on the possibility of selling wheat to Australia. A week ago the hon. minister apparently did not know there was a shortage of wheat in one of the Australian provinces, the state of New South Wales. Back home some of my erstwhile newspaper friends have been taking me to task for the statements I made at that time. I would like to quote an editorial appearing in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix on Wednesday, October 23 under the heading "Homework First":
As a rule, not too much is demanded of freshman members of parliament attending their first session of the commons. Other members and the public generally expect little more from them than a maiden speech and a few timely questions of concern to their constituents.
The new C.C.F. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, Mr. "Scoop" Lewry, evidently is not satisfied with such modest demands, at least he didn't appear to be up until the other day when he was effectively "scooped".
The editorial goes on to say:
He wondered if Canada could not accept sterling instead of dollars from Australia in exchange for Canadian wheat shipped to that country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL
speechtext: I might remind the hon. member that if he wishes to spare his own feelings he can well take refuge in the fact that it is out of order to read an editorial commenting on his previous speech in this session.

maintopic: BASIS NO. 4 NORTHERN-STREET PRICE OF 1.085 PER BUSHEL

May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the editorial takes me to task for my previous remarks by suggesting that I might as profitably have proposed shipping coal to Drumheller or oil to Leduc, that Australia does not import wheat.
Now my own local newspaper likewise took me to task for the statements made on that occasion but two days later the press carried a dispatch from Reuters in Perth Australia, indicating that the situation was as I indicated a week or so before, namely that Australia is in the position where she now wishes to import wheat. There was a news story on October 25 in the Regina Leader-Post stating that once approval is given in Australia for the importation of wheat, preferably from Canada, negotiations will begin about meeting the costs. My question at the time was as to whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce had considered the possibility of selling wheat to Australia. The situation I suggest is known to experts in the grain business, including the Canadian wheat board and the grain division of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but apparently not to the minister nor to some of the newspapers in spite of news stories they themselves carried. It appears virtually certain that Australia will be importing wheat during this current crop year and my purpose in asking the question of the minister was to express the hope that our sister commonwealth would import that wheat from Canada.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix and the Moose Jaw Times-Herald will all do their homework to ascertain the situation in regard to wheat market possibilities, especially within our commonwealth.

intend to speak at length on this bill because I am in general agreement with it. There are however one or two details upon which I would like to comment and upon which I would like clarification. Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the government for keeping this bill simple and for not tying it up with too much red tape. I think, too, that it is good to have the elevator agents do the work of advancing this money. Certainly all hon. members who come from western Canada and who have had dealings with the Canadian wheat board know that the elevator agents keep a close check on the amount of grain that each farmer is storing on his farm. They ask from time to time how much is left, partly I imagine in order that they may report to their companies. Certainly they are well acquainted with this information, so I think the present arrangement is a good one.
One other thing is, I believe, worthy of mention. The advancing of this money is going to place an extra load on elevator agents and I certainly hope that the grain companies will take this into consideration and adjust their pay in recognition of the extra work that is to be done.
Mention is made in the bill of the fact that all money which a farmer has borrowed under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act must be repaid before he can take home any of the money that is being advanced under the terms of this bill. I think that is a little harsh, because many of the farmers will not have a sufficiently large quota to enable them to repay their loans with the amount of money that is being advanced under this plan, namely 50 cents in the case of wheat, 35 cents in the case of barley and 20 cents in the case of oats. We must bear in mind that the amounts per bushel to be advanced will in fact constitute less than 50 per cent of the value of those grains, and I think that the balance of the value of those grains should be considered in demanding payment, that is, the last cent of the payment, due in respect of loans under the interim financing act.
One other thing seems unfair to me. Under the present provisions, if a tenant and a landlord hold a joint permit book, as is often the case, the tenant cannot take out an advance unless the landlord also applies. There will no doubt be cases where a landlord may not need an advance on grain that is being stored on the farm. There may also be cases where a landlord is away from the district and not available to make a joint application with his tenant. In such cases it would appear to me that if the tenant requires an advance and the landlord is either unable or unwilling to apply with him the tenant should be in a position to take advantage of this measure.

erroneous impression. There have been suggestions that this is a.handout or a subsidy. There are things that a government can do to help depressed sections of our agriculture industry without great cost to the taxpayers and here, I think, is a typical example.

Restrictive trade practices adopted by the United States government in its give-away programs have taken from us many of our grain markets. The result is that our exports have decreased.
There has been a major increase in production due to efficient farming and good weather conditions and the situation has become aggravated until it has reached the point where the available storage in this country no longer holds our production. There has been plugging and congestion all along the line. Interior storage is also congested and this has worked back to the farms. Most farmers have hundreds and in some cases thousands of bushels of wheat on their farms and the land is producing more. Many millions of bushels of grain must lie in the open field which is a criminal situation.
It is not the job of the farmer to sell his grain. That responsibility rests with the Department of Trade and Commerce of the federal government. I want to congratulate this government for recognizing its responsibility.
In principle this bill says that if a farmer is unable to deliver his grain through no fault of his own then the government will allow him to receive an advance. I would like to point out to those who have spoken against the bill that this does not in any way add one dollar of income to the net return of any producer; we are giving him nothing. Through this measure the government is merely recognizing in some degree that this is one step it can take in making some money available to the farmer in advance for the grain he is expected to produce in the next six or eight months.
The government is calling upon the people of Canada to aid in bearing a portion of the cost which will amount to the interest on the money which they are going to have to advance to the farmer. What else should they do? Surely this is but little. In this bill the government is recognizing the responsibility the previous government refused to accept. The present government feels the farmer should not be compelled to bear the burden caused by the failures and errors of other people.
If the farmers of western Canada lived in the United States just 100 miles south, for instance, they would receive 90 per cent of the value of their wheat as soon as it was threshed. The government of that country is providing storage so spoilage will not occur. There is a price support program in that country protecting the farmers' produce which eases the worry of bankruptcy. Hundreds of Canadian farmers are facing bankruptcy. Family farms are being ruined in many areas.
As everyone who lives in that part of the country knows, if an individual farmer has to store his own grain and all storage facilities are filled the grain may spoil. It may get damp if the farmer has difficulty in turning it over and keeping it dry. This is good food, the result of man's labour and favourable weather conditions; surely it should be treated as a blessing to a hungry world.
I advocated in this house some four years ago that the government should undertake the building of proper storage facilities, both inland and seaboard. I said that if the conditions prevailing in 1954 continued they would result in deliveries being reduced to a mere trickle and asked the government to take action at that time to provide adequate facilities where the grain could be stored

until it could be sold or until some means could be found for supplying it to hungry people and thus maintain the agricultural industry in a healthy condition.

maintopic: FINAL STATEMENT

speechtext:
The meeting of commonwealth prime ministers was concluded to-day. This was the first commonwealth meeting at which Ghana was represented, following her attainment of independence in March, 1957. Other commonwealth ministers welcomed Ghana's participation in the meeting as a full member of the commonwealth, and took note of this occasion as further practical evidence of the progress made by the United Kingdom government in the pursuit of their policy of fostering constitutional development in their dependent territories.
In the course of their discussions the commonwealth ministers have reviewed all the major international questions of the day which are of common concern to their countries. In this association of free and independent nations it is inevitable that there should be some differences of viewpoint and opinion. But these meetings reveal a broad similarity of approach and purpose. It is not their function, nor is it the object of this communique, to record agreed decisions or formal resolutions. Their value lies in the opportunity which they afford for a full and candid exchange of views in the light of which each commonwealth government can formulate and pursue its separate policies with deeper knowledge and understanding of the views and interests of its fellow members.
The primary objective of all commonwealth governments is world peace and security. They believe that this objective can only be assured by increased co-operation between nations. They themselves accept the principle and practice of co-operation; it is the foundation of their own association. They will continue to work for its wider adoption.
The United Nations was designed to provide one of the main opportunities for the practical exercise of the principle of co-operation between nations. Experience has, however, revealed certain deficiencies and weaknesses in the functioning of the organization. The commonwealth ministers agreed that constructive action is needed to strengthen and improve the United Nations as an instrument for preserving peace, justice and co-operation throughout the world in accordance with the principles of the charter.
In discussion of developments since their last meeting, commonwealth ministers expressed their grave concern at the' tragic events in Hungary. They took note that the forthcoming consideration by the general
assembly of the report presented by its special committee will provide the occasion for the United Nations to record its views.
Commonwealth ministers reviewed the course of the developments in the current discussions on disarmament. They noted that proposals relating to a first stage of disarmament were put forward on 2nd July in the disarmament subcommittee on behalf of the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and France. They recognized that even a limited agreement, by reducing the suspicions and tensions throughout the world, would help to create conditions in which a more comprehensive scheme of disarmament could be developed.
The commonwealth ministers discussed the international problems of the Middle East. They agreed that, in the long term, economic and social progress must be the foundation for stability in the Middle East. They agreed, however, that in the short term the need is to work toward a relaxation of the tension arising from the dispute between the Arab states and Israel, the plight of the Arab refugees and the unresolved problems in connection with the Suez canal. They considered that solutions of all these urgent questions should continue to be pursued by all practicable means.
Consideration was also given to the contribution which might be made by the commonwealth governments concerned toward the easing of tension and the maintenance of peace, stability and political freedom in the Far East and southeast Asia. Commonwealth ministers welcomed the important contribution already made by mutual assistance under the Colombo plan toward raising standards of living and promoting economic development in the underdeveloped countries of this area.
In their general review of economic questions the commonwealth ministers gave special attention to the impact of the major programs of development on which many of their countries are now engaged. These programs call for high levels of domestic saving which can only be secured by sound internal policies. But they also call for conditions favourable to investment from other countries. The United Kingdom will continue to play its leading role in furthering economic development in the countries of the commonwealth, and important contributions are also being made by other commonwealth members. But, in view of the continued need for capital investment, it is also important to encourage

investment from other sources on suitable conditions.
The commonwealth ministers noted the progress made since their last meeting toward the freeing of trade and payments. In this context they discussed the proposals for the creation of an industrial free trade area in Europe as a complement to the European economic community to be set up under the treaty of Rome. They agreed that, as part of the continuous exchange of views between commonwealth governments on these matters, particular aspects of the proposals which might specially affect certain countries of the commonwealth should be examined in London next week by officials of all commonwealth countries in the light of the ministers' discussions.
The commonwealth ministers noted that the annual meeting of the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development will be held in Washington in September. The normal practice is for this meeting to be followed by a meeting of commonwealth finance ministers. The Prime Minister of Canada extended an invitation that this meeting of finance ministers should be held this year in Ottawa.
The commonwealth ministers recognized the value of the work carried out over the past
thirty years by the commonwealth economic committee. They agreed that the committee should be invited to examine and suggest to governments what expansion of its scope and functions might usefully be undertaken for the particular purpose of drawing attention to the economic resources of commonwealth countries.
The commonwealth ministers reviewed the progress of co-operation within the commonwealth in the use of nuclear energy for civil purposes. They recognized the growing importance of the contribution which nuclear energy can make to the peaceful development of their countries and of the rest of the world and the value of close collaboration between members of the commonwealth in this field. For this purpose nuclear scientists from commonwealth countries will be invited to an informal meeting in the United Kingdom in 1958.
The commonwealth ministers noted that the federation of Malaya was on the eve of attaining independence. They extended to the federation their warm good wishes for its future, and they looked forward to being able to welcome an independent Malaya as a member of the commonwealth on the completion of the necessary constitutional processes.
